facts.fact: The University of Tasmania researchers behind the wombat-poo study won the 2019 Ig Nobel Physics Prize.
The 2019 Ig Nobel prizes were whittled down from approximately 9,000 nominations.
To see how the gut makes the cubes, researchers inflated a piece of the last section of a wombat's intestine with a small balloon.
Bare-nosed wombats may poop up to 100 cubes a day; the cubes are about 2 centimeters in size.
Scientists suspect the cube shape lets wombats mark their territory on rocks and logs with poop that won't easily roll away.

Every 30 to 60 seconds, all penguins in the huddle make small 5 to 10 cm steps that travel through the huddle as a wave.

facts.fact: Raccoons are nocturnal: they spend most daylight hours in trees and come down at night to search for food.
Research has shown that food-dousing (dipping food in water) only occurs in raccoons raised in captivity; it has nothing to do with cleanliness or moistening the food.
Raccoon paws contain highly developed nerves, and water actually makes their paws more sensitive.
Raccoons weigh 10 to 30 pounds; records exist of raccoons weighing up to 40 pounds.
Raccoon tails have 4 to 6 black rings.

facts.fact: The 2017 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics went to a study using fluid dynamics to probe the question 'Can a cat be both a solid and a liquid?'
The paper 'On the rheology of cats' was published in the Rheology Bulletin in July 2014.
A liquid is traditionally defined as a material that adapts its shape to fit a container; cats can adapt their shape to their container if we give them enough time.
In rheology the relaxation time is divided by the observation time (the Deborah number): more than 1 means relatively solid, less than 1 means relatively liquid.

facts.fact: Scientists analysed a shred of 68-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex protein (collagen) along with that of 21 modern species; the work was published in Science (Harvard report of April 24, 2008).
They had only 6 peptides, just 89 amino acids, from T. rex.
T. rex grouped with birds (ostrich and chicken) better than any other organism studied, and better than modern reptiles such as alligators and green anole lizards.
An earlier 2007 study used mass spectrometry to obtain protein sequences from bones of a 68-million-year-old T. rex.

facts.fact: The three-toed sloth has an average ground speed of 1.8 to 2.4 m (6 to 8 ft) per minute, and in the trees it can 'accelerate' to 4.6 m (15 ft) per minute.
A three-toed sloth descends its tree weekly (about once every 7 days) to defecate.
Sloths spend most of their time resting or eating in the forest canopy, and they eat algae that grow in their own fur.

facts.fact: Using high-speed video and flow-rate measurements at Zoo Atlanta, researchers found that all mammals above 3 kg empty their bladders over a nearly constant 21 ± 13 seconds.
Larger animals have longer urethras and thus higher gravitational force and flow speed, so the urinary system scales up by a factor of 3,600 in volume without losing its function.
Smaller mammals are limited by viscous and capillary forces, so their urine comes out as single drops.
The study won the 2015 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics, for testing that nearly all mammals empty their bladders in about 21 seconds (plus or minus 13 seconds).

facts.fact: Dung beetles roll their dung balls along straight paths under a starlit sky but lose this ability under overcast conditions.

In a planetarium the beetles oriented equally well under a full starlit sky as when only the Milky Way was shown; it is the first documented use of the Milky Way for orientation in the animal kingdom.
In the outdoor test the beetles rolled from a dung pile to a ring with a radius of about 4 feet; with tiny blinders on their eyes their paths became much windier.
With only 18 of the brightest stars switched on, their paths became significantly windier.
The study won the 2013 Ig Nobel Prize in Biology and Astronomy.

facts.fact: Sea otters have the world's densest fur: at its thickest, more than 1 million hairs per square inch (per 1 square inch); a person has probably 100,000 hairs or less on the whole head.
An otter's coat has pockets: loose skin under each forearm that it uses to stash prey during a dive.
If dinner is a crab or clam, the otter may use a rock to crack it open.
A sea otter eats about a quarter of its body weight each day.

facts.fact: To conserve energy, koalas sleep 18 to 22 hours a day.
Koalas don't get many calories from their eucalypt leaf diet, so they conserve energy by moving only occasionally.
Eucalypt leaves have strong-smelling oils that make koalas smell a bit like menthol cough drops.

facts.fact: A duckling swimming at a 'sweet point' behind its mother is actually pushed forward by the mother's wave (wave-riding).
The study was published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics and announced by the University of Strathclyde on 6 October 2021.
Starting from the third duckling (3rd in the line), the wave drag of each duckling gradually tends towards 0, and each one passes the wave energy on to the next.
The work won the 2022 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics, for trying to understand how ducklings manage to swim in formation.

facts.fact: Captured black rhinoceroses have been moved by air by suspending them by their feet.
12 wild black rhinoceroses (median weight 1,137 kg) were tested lying on their side and hanging by their feet from a crane, for about 10 minutes each.
Hanging by the feet for 10 minutes did not impair lung function more than lying on the side, and slightly improved gas exchange.
The study won the 2021 Ig Nobel Prize in Transportation, for determining by experiment whether it is safer to transport an airborne rhinoceros upside-down.

facts.fact: The peacock mantis shrimp swings its club-shaped front leg at peak speeds of 23 meters per second (measured peaks ranged from 14 to 23 meters per second).
The strike was filmed at 5,000 frames per second.
Peak accelerations ranged from 6,300 to 8,000 times that of gravity.
The blow yields force well over 100 times the mantis shrimp's body weight.
